text: In everyday life, people often perform cognitive activities while walking, communicating, using electronic devices, or processing environmental information, making cognitive-motor dual-tasking a common behavioral phenomenon ( Al-Yahya et al., 2011 ). A cognitive-motor dual-task refers to the simultaneous performance of cognitive and motor tasks ( Watanabe and Funahashi, 2018 ). Experimental studies show that dual-tasking requires dynamic allocation of limited cognitive resources, and increased cognitive load may impair cognitive and motor performance due to resource competition ( Schaefer, 2014 ). fNIRS studies indicate that higher cognitive load during cognitive-motor dual-task walking is associated with reduced cognitive performance, slower gait speed, and increased prefrontal cortex (PFC) activation ( Rahman et al., 2021 ), along with coordinated changes in motor-related brain regions, suggesting involvement of distributed brain networks ( Ou et al., 2024 ). Therefore, cognitive-motor dual-task processing involves coordinated interactions across multiple brain regions rather than a single region. The PFC, particularly the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), plays a key role in cognitive control and task regulation ( Yang et al., 2013 ; Chen et al., 2026 ), while the primary motor cortex (M1) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC) contribute to motor control and sensory integration during dual-task performance ( Lim et al., 2022 ). Overall, examining brain activation and network-level changes under different cognitive loads is essential for understanding its neural mechanisms.
source_label: Cortical activation and functional connectivity during dual-task walking under different cognitive loads: an fNIRS study
